Tessl Verifiers 是用纯文本编写的规则，存放在你的仓库中，并在每次代码变更时进行检查。每次运行时，它们都会返回通过或失败，因此你可以像今天使用 lint 或测试一样使用 verifiers：在本地、在 pre-commit 中，或作为 CI 门禁。它们适用于 linter 无法检查的规则，例如“面向用户的错误必须告诉用户下一步该做什么”。

blocks.text: 我们为什么构建它们
大多数团队已经为他们的 agent 编写了编码标准。也许他们规定了应该使用哪个 helper，或者哪些 API 应该和不应该被调用，当然还有安全最佳实践，比如绝不记录 token。Agent 通常能很好地遵循这些规则，但它们不会每次都捕捉到所有问题。当某条规则被遗漏时，你通常要到代码审查时才会发现，甚至更晚。

inlines.text: 大多数团队已经为他们的 agent 编写了编码标准。也许他们规定了应该使用哪个 helper，或者哪些 API 应该和不应该被调用，当然还有安全最佳实践，比如绝不记录 token。Agent 通常能很好地遵循这些规则，但它们不会每次都捕捉到所有问题。当某条规则被遗漏时，你通常要到代码审查时才会发现，甚至更晚。

blocks.text: Linters 无法帮助处理大多数这类规则，因为它们只能检查确定性规则。AI 代码审查可以捕捉到它们，但审查会查找 PR 中的一般性问题，并不能在每次运行时可靠地检查同一条规则。在 Tessl，我们需要介于两者之间的东西：一种既能理解你的代码，又能保证每次确定性地运行相同规则的检查。

Tessl Verifiers are rules written in plain text that live in your repo, and are checked on every code change. Each time they run, they return a pass or fail, so you can use verifiers the same way you use lint or tests today: locally, in pre-commit, or as a CI gate. They're meant for rules a linter can't check, like "user-facing errors must tell the user what to do next."

blocks.text: Why we built them

Most teams already have written coding standards for their agents. Perhaps they state which helper should be used, or which APIs should and shouldn't be called, and of course security best practices like never log a token. Agents often follow these rules well, but they won't catch everything, every time. When a rule slips, you usually won't find out till code review, or even later.

inlines.text: Most teams already have written coding standards for their agents. Perhaps they state which helper should be used, or which APIs should and shouldn't be called, and of course security best practices like never log a token. Agents often follow these rules well, but they won't catch everything, every time. When a rule slips, you usually won't find out till code review, or even later.

blocks.text: Linters can't help with most of these rules, because theycan check deterministic rules. AI code review can catch them, but review looks for general problems across a PR and won't reliably check the same rule on every run. At Tessl, we needed something in between: a check that both understands your code, and deterministically runs the same rules every time, guaranteed.

blocks.text: How they work

A verifier is a JSON file in your repo. It holds an instruction, the conditions for when it applies, and a checklist of yes-or-no rules. When you run tessl change verify, an LLM judge reads the relevant files and scores each rule as pass or fail.

inlines.text: A verifier is a JSON file in your repo. It holds an instruction, the conditions for when it applies, and a checklist of yes-or-no rules. When you run
, an LLM judge reads the relevant files and scores each rule as pass or fail.

blocks.text: The files a verifier applies for, and how strict it is, is set in the verify block of tessl.json. Each group gets a level of info, warn or error. In CI, warnings are reported but don't fail the build. Errors exit non-zero and can block the PR. Because scope and severity live outside the verifier itself, you can reuse one verifier across teams with different settings.

blocks.text: When to use one

A verifier is a good fit when the rule has a clear yes-or-no answer, you can see the evidence in the changed files, and no linter or test can check it reliably. If a linter can do the job, use the linter.

blocks.text: Verifiers don't work well for subjective questions like "is this readable?" Narrow the rule until you could check it with a checklist.

blocks.text: It helps to think of verifiers alongside the other tools you already use. A rule tells an agent what to do before it writes code. A verifier checks the result afterwards. They work well as a pair: the rule teaches the pattern, and the verifier catches the cases where the agent didn't follow it.
